title: A single-absorber solar converter that uses non-thermal carriers to pass the detailed-balance limit

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a solar converter with one light-absorbing material and one bandgap that captures useful electrical energy from excited charge carriers before they lose that energy to the material’s lattice as heat. Its target is reproducible conversion above the applicable detailed-balance limit for a conventional device whose carriers have thermalized to the lattice, under AM1.5G sunlight at one sun and a measured cell temperature of 25 °C. This is a scientific target; the supplied evidence does not establish that it has been achieved.

Conceptual synthesis: in the hot-carrier version, electrons and holes can redistribute energy among themselves and form a carrier population hotter than the lattice. The device must turn that retained carrier free energy into electrical work through extraction, rather than merely exhibit hot carriers. Exceeding a thermalized-carrier benchmark would exploit a different operating regime and its associated assumptions; it would not invalidate thermodynamics or detailed balance. The central distinction is useful extraction before energy loss to the lattice.

significance.text: Conditional significance: verified non-thermal extraction would establish an additional route to higher solar conversion efficiency from a single absorber. At the same incident sunlight, greater efficiency directly means more electrical output per illuminated cell area. A small but reproducible excess with a demonstrated mechanism would therefore be scientifically meaningful even before a commercially useful device existed.

Higher output per cell area could eventually reduce deployment area and electricity cost, but those consequences require scalable manufacturing, suitable optical and system design, reliability, and favorable economics. Cell efficiency alone does not determine total installation land use or delivered electricity cost. The research’s suggestion of avoiding epitaxial multi-junction stacks is best understood as a possible architectural benefit of using one absorber, not evidence that the resulting device would necessarily be simpler or cheaper.

The distinction from existing high-efficiency photovoltaics is essential. Fraunhofer’s documented 47.6 percent device uses four junctions and concentrated illumination, providing a demonstrated route through several absorber bandgaps. That achievement does not demonstrate the proposed extraction of non-thermal carrier energy from one absorber. Likewise, a fractional laboratory excess would establish the principle only if its mechanism and measurement were convincing; it would not by itself establish manufacturability or broad practical transformation.

missing_breakthrough.text: Scientific target and engineering synthesis: the missing capability is an operating single-absorber device that both preserves non-thermal carrier free energy and extracts it as electrical work quickly enough to exceed a properly matched thermalized-carrier limit. Preserving a hot population, observing slow cooling, and obtaining an efficiency excess are individually insufficient to establish the whole capability. The measurements must connect energy retention, extraction dynamics, and delivered electrical power.

Inferred design barriers include maintaining a useful departure from lattice equilibrium under one-sun illumination at 25 °C, making contacts that extract the retained energy without dissipating it, and sustaining useful current and voltage together. Carrier cooling, recombination, contact losses, and transport losses must be controlled in the operating device. These are requirements inferred from the proposed mechanism, rather than experimentally quantified barriers established by the retained sources; the supplied evidence does not identify a material or contact architecture that has solved them.

A further barrier is establishing what an apparent excess actually means. The comparison must use consistent illumination, optical concentration, emission geometry, temperature, and efficiency-area definitions. Mechanism-sensitive measurements must show that extracted non-thermal free energy accounts for the excess, rather than leaving it attributable to an unmatched baseline or measurement uncertainty. This requires a stronger demonstration than a carrier-temperature or spectroscopic signature alone.

current_state.text: Fraunhofer ISE announced on 30 May 2022 that a four-junction solar cell reached 47.6 percent efficiency at 665 suns. The supplied manuscript by Höhn and colleagues, published in the 2024 IEEE Photovoltaic Specialists Conference proceedings, reports 47.6 percent under 665-fold concentration of the AM1.5d spectrum. The announcement date and manuscript publication date are distinct. This is a documented multi-junction concentrator achievement, outside the proposed single-absorber, AM1.5G, one-sun operating conditions.

A 26 September 2025 pv magazine report describes claimed silicon-cell efficiencies of 50–60 percent at cryogenic temperatures of 30–50 K, with internal confirmation and no third-party certification. The article mentions monochromatic laser experiments and separately describes approximately 51 percent under conditions it calls standard illumination. The supplied review finds that the report does not resolve the illumination protocol for that figure, so the result should not be reduced to a precisely established laser-only measurement. It remains a reported experimental claim, not independently validated evidence of the proposed capability at 25 °C.

The research attributes an AM1.5G detailed-balance maximum of 33.16 percent at a bandgap of 1.34 eV to Rühle’s 2016 Solar Energy paper. It also attributes a theoretical 66 percent flat-plate hot-carrier conversion result, compared with approximately 33 percent for an equilibrium device, to Ross and Nozik’s 1982 Journal of Applied Physics paper. Neither paper’s text was retained in the supplied evidence. These figures are therefore preserved as unverified source attributions, not established numerical ceilings for this record. In particular, the 66 percent figure is a theoretical projection whose assumptions remain unverified here, not a demonstrated efficiency or a universally applicable target.

The research also describes an NREL/NLR research-cell chart revised on 12 May 2026 and states that its maximum is 47.6 percent. No retained chart or page text was supplied, so neither the revision date nor its claimed maximum can be verified from this record. The supported historical Fraunhofer result does not establish what the chart contained in 2026.

Evidence boundary: the supplied review had complete, untruncated texts for the Fraunhofer announcement, the three-page conference manuscript, and the cryogenic-silicon press report. Its account of the manuscript’s numerical result rests on extracted prose and does not require interpreting its figures. The theoretical papers and research-cell chart were not captured, and the freshness search record was empty. Consequently, the evidence neither establishes an independently certified standard-conditions hot-carrier demonstration nor supports a universal claim that none exists as of 1 November 2026. Missing evidence is not evidence that a reported result is false.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed scientific demonstration: operate one absorber with one bandgap under AM1.5G illumination at 1000 W m⁻² and a measured cell temperature of 25 °C. Before testing, specify the applicable thermalized-carrier detailed-balance baseline for that bandgap, including spectrum, optical concentration, emission geometry, and the area used to calculate efficiency. An independent photovoltaics laboratory should certify an efficiency at least five percentage points above that baseline, with uncertainty too small to explain the excess. The five-percentage-point margin is a proposed convincing threshold, not an established scientific standard; a smaller excess could still establish the principle if its uncertainty and mechanism were resolved.
completion_criteria.label: Certified efficiency at least five percentage points above detailed-balance baseline

completion_criteria.text: Proposed mechanism test: combine spectroscopy or carrier-temperature measurements with extraction dynamics and electrical measurements on an operating device. Together, these should establish that non-thermal carrier free energy is extracted before loss to the lattice and accounts for the measured efficiency excess. Merely detecting carriers hotter than the lattice would not satisfy this requirement, because a hot population need not deliver additional useful electrical work.
completion_criteria.label: Non-thermal carrier extraction accounts for the measured efficiency excess

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and scope: a second cell of at least 1 cm² should repeat the result under the same specified conditions, with sufficient disclosure for independent reproduction of the device and measurement. The area threshold is a proposal. Such tests would demonstrate performance over the tested devices and operating conditions, not across all materials, illumination spectra, temperatures, or device sizes. Module lifetime lies beyond the initial scientific completion test; manufacturing yield, scalable area, long-term stability, and system economics would remain separate requirements for practical deployment.
completion_criteria.label: Second cell ≥1 cm² reproduces results with sufficient reproduction disclosure

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: THR-01, “A computable thermodynamic potential for far-from-equilibrium continuum transport,” and THR-11, “Operational temperature and entropy for far-from-equilibrium matter,” overlap with the description of non-equilibrium carriers and their available free energy. THR-01 seeks a general predictive transport framework, while THR-11 concerns the meaning and measurement of temperature and entropy away from equilibrium. THR-06 instead requires a particular solar device to extract electrical work; it would not automatically establish either broader theory.

Roster-based synthesis: THR-02, “Useful heat engines that are simultaneously efficient, powerful, and steady,” shares the challenge of converting energy efficiently while delivering sustained power. THR-04, “Bulk electronic heat–charge decoupling sufficient for engine-class solid-state conversion,” shares concerns about heat loss and charge transport. THR-06 specifically targets non-thermal photocarrier extraction from one absorber; it does not by itself demonstrate bulk heat–charge decoupling or the broader heat-engine capability.

Roster-based synthesis: THR-05, “A size-extensive quantum advantage in thermodynamic performance,” could overlap if quantum effects helped retain or extract carrier energy. However, hot-carrier operation does not by itself demonstrate a quantum advantage, much less one that scales extensively with system size. The proposed THR-06 demonstration is defined by its energy-conversion mechanism and efficiency, without requiring that additional claim.

Roster-based synthesis: THR-03, “General-purpose digital computation near the Landauer scale,” and THR-08, “Equilibrium sampling computers operating near thermal energy per sample,” also concern useful operations constrained by thermodynamics. Their outputs are computation and samples, respectively. THR-06 produces electrical work from sunlight and provides no direct demonstration of either computing capability.

Roster-based synthesis: THR-07, “Synthetic chemomechanical engines whose efficiency approaches biological molecular motors,” THR-09, “A thermodynamic design theory of self-replicators, confirmed by a predicted non-biological replicator,” and THR-12, “Predictive thermodynamic design of far-from-equilibrium chemical reaction networks,” share the use of driven systems and controlled dissipation. Their targets are molecular motion, replication, and chemical-network behavior. THR-06 concerns semiconductor photocarriers, so these remain distinct innovations. THR-10, “A laboratory measurement of the Unruh temperature,” has only a broad connection through thermodynamics and temperature measurement; it does not supply the device capability or completion test sought here.

unresolved_issues: The exact assumptions and numerical applicability of the Rühle and Ross–Nozik calculations remain unverified because their texts were not supplied.
The purported 12 May 2026 research-cell chart revision and 47.6 percent maximum remain unverified.
Whether an independently certified single-absorber demonstration meets the proposed operating conditions as of 1 November 2026 remains undetermined.
The cryogenic-silicon report leaves the illumination protocol for approximately 51 percent unresolved; its reported efficiencies lack third-party certification in the supplied account.
A specific absorber, extraction architecture, quantitative cooling and extraction requirements, and validated causal diagnostic have not been established by the supplied evidence.
The exact baseline calculation and measurement protocol must be specified before the proposed completion test can be applied; the five-percentage-point and 1 cm² thresholds remain proposals.

brief.title: Solar cells that capture energy before it becomes heat
possible: You could get more electricity from the same patch of sunlight. A solar cell would use a single light-absorbing material to collect energy that conventional cells lose as heat, exceeding their theoretical efficiency limit under ordinary sunlight at 25 °C.
why: This would establish another route to higher solar efficiency using a single absorbing material. More electrical output from the same cell area could eventually help reduce the space and cost needed to generate solar power.

sources.not_established: A theoretical benchmark does not demonstrate a device that extracts energy before it becomes heat.

sources.showed: This is theoretical work on solar converters that collect energy from excited electrical charges before those charges cool.
sources.cited_for: It supports the theoretical case for collecting energy otherwise lost as heat.
sources.not_established: The calculation does not demonstrate an operating solar cell.

Researchers at the University of Delaware and Taizhou University reported high efficiency in deeply cooled silicon cells. That claim lacks independent certification and does not establish the proposed capability at room temperature.
missing: An operating cell must retain extra energy in excited electrical charges and extract it as electricity before it becomes heat.
Independent measurements must establish an efficiency excess against a limit calculated for matching test conditions.
Measurements must connect the retained energy, its extraction and the additional electrical power.
Another cell must reproduce the result with enough detail for independent reproduction.

milestones.label: Certified efficiency five percentage points above the matched limit
milestones.explanation: An independent laboratory would have to certify that margin for a single absorbing material with a single absorption-energy threshold under the specified sunlight and temperature. Measurement uncertainty must not explain the excess.

milestones.label: Extracted energy explains the extra electrical output
milestones.explanation: Measurements of excited charges, extraction speed and electrical output would have to show that retained energy explains the efficiency excess. Detecting charges hotter than the surrounding material would not suffice.

milestones.label: Another cell reproduces the result over a square centimetre
milestones.explanation: Another cell of at least 1 cm² would have to repeat the result under the same conditions, with enough detail for independent reproduction. This would establish repeatability over the tested devices.

uncertain: The exact efficiency limit depends on the absorber and matched assumptions about illumination, temperature and light emission.
Which absorbing material and electrical contacts can retain and extract enough energy remains unresolved.
The proposed efficiency margin and minimum cell area are judging thresholds, rather than established scientific standards.

page.title: Hot-carrier solar cells beyond the Shockley–Queisser limit
page.definition: A solar cell with one absorbing material and one bandgap—the minimum electron–hole excitation energy—extracts electrical work from excited charges before their excess energy becomes heat. Under standard terrestrial sunlight (AM1.5G), at one sun and 25 °C, its efficiency exceeds the matched detailed-balance limit for charges equilibrated with the atomic lattice.

goal.need: Photons above a semiconductor's absorption threshold create carriers with excess energy that ordinarily heats the lattice. Ross and Nozik's idealized AM1.5, 300 K calculation gives a factor-of-two efficiency difference between thermal-equilibrium and hot-carrier converters. Recovering that energy as electrical work is the goal; the calculated efficiencies are not device results.

figures.caption: Calculated flat-plate conversion efficiencies in the Ross–Nozik model
figures.note: AM1.5 illumination at 300 K. These theoretical optima are not completion thresholds.

statements.context: The laboratory describes developing and validating a slow-cooling absorber and energy-selective contacts separately before integrating them. Energy-selective contacts transmit carriers within a restricted energy range.

completion.title: A single-absorber cell exceeds its matched thermalized-carrier limit through hot-carrier extraction.
completion.criterion: An independent, recognized photovoltaic laboratory confirms that a cell with one absorbing material and one bandgap exceeds its radiative, thermalized-carrier detailed-balance efficiency ceiling under AM1.5G illumination at 1000 W m⁻² and measured cell temperature 25 °C. The ceiling uses the same bandgap, spectrum, optical concentration and emission geometry; efficiency uses total or aperture area. Measurement uncertainty cannot explain the excess. Device measurements and peer-reviewed analysis establish that extraction of retained carrier energy accounts for the excess.
completion.set_by: Atlas synthesis of the published hot-carrier device goal and photovoltaic measurement conventions; no adopted test combining these requirements was located.
completion.basis: Searched ARENA hot-carrier project documents, IEC 60904 measurement documents, NLR record rules, and experimental and review literature for an adopted above-limit, one-sun hot-carrier test; none was located. This test combines the complete-device goal with standard photovoltaic conditions and independent efficiency confirmation. It imposes no fixed efficiency margin or minimum cell area.

milestones.title: An absorber sustains a carrier population hotter than its lattice under continuous illumination.
milestones.criterion: Under continuous excitation, the absorber sustains a carrier temperature above the lattice temperature. NextPV reported InGaAs/AlGaAs quantum-well carrier temperatures of 520 K under 532 nm excitation equivalent to 40,000 suns in room-temperature experiments. Sourabh et al. reported hot-carrier luminescence in a mixed-halide perovskite cell at 100 K under elevated laser excitation. These results concern high carrier injection.
milestones.set_by: Hot-carrier absorber criterion stated by NextPV in Almosni et al., section 2.3.1; its experimental examples concern III–V heterostructures.
milestones.threshold_quote: a stable population at a temperature higher than that of the lattice.

milestones.title: Energy-selective extraction removes hot carriers from an absorber before they cool to its band edges.
milestones.criterion: Extraction removes carriers with excess energy before that energy is transferred to the lattice. Dimmock et al. demonstrated resonant hot-electron extraction from GaAs under 790–810 nm excitation at 93 K. Gong et al. reported perovskite hot-hole extraction at 78,900 cm s⁻¹ over approximately 79 nm. The latter result addresses extraction speed; it does not by itself establish the energy selectivity of a complete hot-carrier cell.
milestones.set_by: Hot-carrier photovoltaic convention originating with Ross and Nozik and experimentally applied by Sharp Laboratories of Europe in Dimmock et al., section 6; that experiment concerns GaAs/AlGaAs.
milestones.threshold_quote: extract photogenerated carriers faster than they can thermalise

milestones.title: An integrated cell converts extracted hot-carrier energy into electrical power.
milestones.criterion: A complete cell supplies net electrical power through hot-carrier extraction, with a measured electrical contribution from retained carrier energy. Dimmock et al. reported a GaAs/AlGaAs cell with about 0.5 V open-circuit voltage and tens of nanoamperes short-circuit current; at 93 K its maximum-power-point voltage changed by at least 0.08 V between 810 and 790 nm excitation. Gong et al. reported 27.30% perovskite efficiency at 5.9 suns and voltage above a modeled cold-carrier line. These results use cryogenic or concentrated illumination.
milestones.set_by: Experimental hot-carrier photovoltaic convention applied by Sharp Laboratories of Europe in Dimmock et al., section 7, and by ARENA/UNSW in its integrated-device outcome. Dimmock's test concerns GaAs/AlGaAs.
milestones.threshold_quote: this tunnelling mechanism gives rise to a photovoltaic effect.

milestones.title: A single-absorber hot-carrier cell supplies electrical power at one sun and 25 °C.
milestones.criterion: One cell supplies a load under AM1.5G illumination at 1000 W m⁻² and measured cell temperature 25 °C, while measurements establish extraction of retained hot-carrier energy in that operating cell. Gong et al.'s certified 24.43% perovskite result establishes one-sun efficiency, but the opened abstract associates its above-cold-carrier voltage result with 5.9 suns. A result establishing this complete test was not located for either tracked absorber class.
milestones.set_by: Atlas synthesis of the complete-device goal and IEC standard test conditions. Searches of programme documents, measurement rules and device literature found no published milestone combining standard conditions with a demonstrated hot-carrier contribution to power.

not_found: No adopted protocol combining above-limit efficiency, hot-carrier attribution, one sun and 25 °C was located.
No independently confirmed result satisfying the completion test was located.
Independent-device replicate counts were not established for the NextPV, Dimmock and Gong results cited here.
Gong et al.'s publisher full text could not be opened; its abstract was available in the laboratory repository.
The publisher full texts of Rühle's 2016 paper and Ross–Nozik's 1982 paper could not be opened; the latter's abstract was available in the laboratory repository.
